lessons.title: NEPSE has no market orders. Everything is a limit order.

blocks.md: You've watched a video where someone taps "Buy" and the trade fills instantly at whatever the price is. You open TMS looking for that button. It isn't there. It has never been there. And once you understand why, you will stop wanting it.

On NEPSE, every order is a [[limit_order|limit order]]. You must name a price. There is no "buy at market" that hands your order to whatever the other side is asking.

A limit order is an instruction with a ceiling or a floor:

- **Buy limit at Rs. 240** means: buy for me at Rs. 240 **or less**. Never more.
- **Sell limit at Rs. 260** means: sell for me at Rs. 260 **or more**. Never less.

Your order goes into the [[order_book|order book]] and sits there, sorted first by price and then by the time it arrived. This is **[[price_time_priority|price–time priority]]**. If you and another buyer both bid Rs. 240 and they got there four seconds earlier, they get filled first. Every share.

Three things follow from this, and they are the difference between a beginner and someone who knows what they are doing.

### Your order may not fill at all

If you bid Rs. 240 and the stock trades all day between Rs. 243 and Rs. 251, you own nothing. That is not a bug. That is you refusing to overpay, which is the correct behaviour.

### Your order may fill partially

You want 500 kitta at Rs. 240. Only 180 are offered at Rs. 240 or below. You get 180. The remaining 320 stay live in the book. And here is the part that costs people money: you pay the [[dp_charge|DP charge]] and the commission on **each settlement**, so a badly-planned order that fills across two days costs you two DP charges instead of one.

### Chasing is expensive

The natural move when your order doesn't fill is to cancel and re-enter higher. Do this three times in a rising market and you have paid a price you would have refused an hour ago. This is why you decide your maximum price **before** you open TMS, and write it down.

There is one exception worth knowing. During the [[pre_open|pre-open session]], orders are collected without matching and a single opening price is calculated that maximises executable volume. As of the April 2026 rules the pre-open band is ±5% from the previous close (it was ±2% before). Orders placed in pre-open all execute at that one discovered price, which is the closest NEPSE gets to a market order.

blocks.md: Order price band during continuous trading is **±3% from the last traded price** (relaxed from ±2% in April 2026), while the daily circuit limit for an individual stock is **±15% from the previous close** (raised from ±10%, effective 21 April 2026). These are two different limits and both apply. The 3% band controls how far from the current price you may place an order; the 15% circuit controls how far the stock may move in the whole day.

bullets: Every NEPSE order is a limit order — you always name a price, and it may not fill.
Matching is by price–time priority; being early in the queue at the same price matters.

lessons.title: Anatomy of an order: symbol, quantity, rate, validity

blocks.md: Four fields. That is the entire order ticket. People still get it wrong, and the two most common mistakes both cost real money — one in fees, one in a price you did not intend to pay.

### Symbol

The NEPSE ticker: NABIL, UPPER, API. Check it twice. Similar codes exist — NICA and NIMB are different banks, SBI and SBL are different banks — and TMS will happily let you buy the wrong one.

### Side

Buy or sell. Selling requires shares already **settled** in your Demat. You cannot sell what arrives on T+2, which is why intraday trading does not exist here.

### Quantity

Expressed in **[[kitta]]**. The usual minimum lot is **10 kitta**, in multiples of 10. Odd lots — quantities that do not fit the lot size, usually created by bonus issues — trade in a separate odd-lot market with far less liquidity.

Quantity is also where the DP charge arithmetic bites. Placing one order for 500 that fills across two days costs Rs. 50 in DP charges; placing an order you expect to fill completely costs Rs. 25.

### Rate

The price. Every order is a [[limit_order|limit order]], so this is your ceiling if buying and your floor if selling. It must sit inside **both** the ±3% band from the LTP and the ±15% circuit from the previous close.

### Validity

NEPSE orders are **day orders**. They expire at the close. There is no good-till-cancelled, so an order you placed on Monday is gone by Tuesday morning and it is on you to place it again.

Since April 2026 you can enter orders **round the clock**; they queue and execute only between 11:00 and 15:00. This is genuinely useful — you can set your price the night before, calmly, rather than at 11:04 with the market moving.

lessons.title: The pre-open session and the 5% band

blocks.md: For a few minutes each morning, NEPSE collects orders and matches none of them. Then it computes a single price and executes everything at once. It is the only moment in the Nepali trading day that behaves like an auction — and the only time you get something close to a market order.

The **[[pre_open|pre-open session]]** runs before continuous trading starts. Orders are collected but not matched. At the end, NEPSE computes one **equilibrium price** — the price at which the greatest volume can execute — and every crossing order fills at that single price.

### Why an auction at the open

Overnight news arrives while the market is shut. If trading simply started at 11:00, the first few orders would set the price in a thin, chaotic minute, and whoever was fastest would capture the difference. Collecting orders first and discovering one price is fairer and less noisy.

### The band

Pre-open orders must sit within **±5% of the previous close**, raised from ±2% in the 2026 rule changes. That is wider than the ±3% continuous-session band and narrower than the ±15% daily circuit — a third limit, applying at a third moment.

### How the equilibrium price is found

For each candidate price, the exchange computes how much volume could execute if that were the price. The price that maximises executable volume wins. Ties are broken by the smallest order imbalance, and then by proximity to the previous close.

### What this means for you

An order placed in pre-open executes at the discovered price, **not necessarily at your limit**. If you bid Rs. 240 and the equilibrium comes out at Rs. 236, you buy at Rs. 236 — better than your limit. That is the closest NEPSE gets to a market order, and it is why pre-open is a reasonable way to enter a liquid stock when you care more about getting filled than about a rupee of price.

On a thin counter it is the opposite: a handful of orders can set an equilibrium price that has nothing to do with where the stock will trade an hour later.

The equilibrium price is **Rs. 231.00** — it maximises executable volume at 2,400 kitta. Everyone who bid Rs. 231 or above buys at Rs. 231; everyone who offered Rs. 231 or below sells at Rs. 231.

Notice what happened to the person who bid Rs. 237: they paid Rs. 231, not Rs. 237. Their limit was a ceiling, and the auction found a better price. Notice also the person who offered at Rs. 228 — they sold at Rs. 231, three rupees better than their floor.

And the honest warning: on a counter where the whole pre-open book is 400 kitta, this same mechanism can print an equilibrium price that no one would pay ten minutes later.

lessons.title: Order book, trade book, and what "partially executed" means

blocks.md: Your order book says 500. Your trade book says 180. You own 180. The gap between those two numbers has caused more miscounted positions than any other feature of TMS.

Two books, two different questions.

The **[[order_book|order book]]** answers *what have I submitted?* The **[[trade_book|trade book]]** answers *what actually executed?* Only the trade book means you own something.

### The five states an order passes through

- **Open** — resting in the queue at your price. Nothing has happened.
- **Partially executed** — some quantity filled; the remainder is still live.
- **Executed** — fully filled. This is the only state that means the whole order is done.
- **Cancelled** — you withdrew it, or the unfilled remainder was withdrawn.
- **Expired** — the close arrived and the unfilled quantity died with it, because NEPSE orders are day orders.

### What partial execution actually costs

This is the part that matters financially. Each **settlement date** attracts its own Rs. 25 [[dp_charge|DP charge]] per company. An order that fills 180 today and 320 tomorrow settles twice:

- Two DP charges instead of one
- Two entries in your [[wacc|WACC]] calculation, at two different prices
- Two settlement dates to track for [[edis|EDIS]] if you later sell

The commission and SEBON fee are proportional, so those do not change. Only the flat charge doubles.

### Reading the book properly

After every submission, check the order book once. "Submitted" is not "executed" — and at the close, check it again, because an unfilled order simply vanishes and it is on you to notice.

lessons.title: Modifying and cancelling: what you can and can't undo

blocks.md: You are fourth in the queue at Rs. 240 with 620 kitta ahead of you. You nudge your price up by fifty paisa to jump the queue. You have just gone to the back of a different queue — and given up your place in the old one for nothing.

### What you can change

While an order is **open** or **partially executed**, you can modify its price or quantity, or cancel the unfilled portion entirely.

### What you cannot change

An **executed** portion is final. If 180 of your 500 filled, those 180 are yours — you cannot cancel them, you can only sell them later as a separate transaction with its own costs and its own capital gains tax.

### The rule that costs people money

**Modifying the price loses your time priority.** Matching is by [[price_time_priority|price then time]]. Change your price and your order re-enters the book at the back of the queue for the new price.

This matters most in exactly the situation where people reach for the modify button — a fast-moving, well-bid stock, where the queue at each price level is long.

Modifying the quantity **downward** generally preserves your place; increasing it does not. The safe assumption is that any modification puts you at the back.

### When cancelling is right

- The reason you wanted the stock has changed — an earnings release, a circular from Nepal Rastra Bank, a disclosure.
- You need the cash for something else.
- You realise you sized the position wrong.

### When cancelling is a mistake

When the only thing that has changed is that the price moved away from you and you want to chase it. That is the behaviour Lesson 5.1 warns about, and it is the single most expensive habit a new NEPSE trader can form. Decide your maximum before you log in, and let the order live or die at that price.

blocks.md: You cannot cancel an executed portion. If part of your order filled, that part is a completed trade with its own contract note, its own commission, its own [[dp_charge|DP charge]] and — when you eventually sell it — its own [[cgt|capital gains tax]] computed from its own lot. Unwinding it means a fresh sale with a fresh round of costs.

blocks.after:
Patience was worth **Rs. 1,705.86** against chasing — 1.42% of the position, on a single decision made in about four seconds.

And the honest other outcome, because the losing case matters: on a different day the stock never dips, your Rs. 240 order expires unfilled, and it closes at Rs. 249. You have "saved" Rs. 1,706 and missed a Rs. 4,500 gain. Both of these happen. The reason patience still wins over a career is not that it always fills better — it is that **chasing has no upper bound and refusing to overpay does**.
